title: Whose is this? Whose are these? Kenen …?
summary: Ask whose one or several things are without adding a personal suffix.
prerequisiteSkills: Plural possessed nouns in ownership sentences
objectives: Ask whose one or several things are without adding a personal suffix.
Apply this rule with the supporting forms shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Kenen means “whose”, an owner-question form of kuka (“who”). The owner is unspecified, so add no personal possessive suffix to the question noun.
For one thing use Kenen + basic noun + tämä on?: Kenen pallo tämä on? (“Whose ball is this?”). For several things keep plural -t: Kenen pallot nämä ovat? (“Whose balls are these?”).

Kenen stays the same merely because several things are named. It does not by itself establish whether one person or several people own them. Explicit questions about several owners are outside this bounded pattern.

Kenen tämä pallo on? and Kenen nämä pallot ovat? are also ordinary word orders. Typed and token tasks accept both orders. An answer naming a personal owner uses that owner’s possessive ending; question-to-answer combination waits for Review.
keyPoints: Ask whose one or several things are without adding a personal suffix.

steps: Begin with Kenen (“whose”) to ask about an unspecified owner.
Use kirja (“book”) without a personal possessive suffix.
Use nämä ovat for several things or tämä on for one thing.

commonMistakes: Do not add a personal suffix to the question noun.
The number of things does not determine the number of owners.
